newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WOODS ROARS BACK INTO HUNT AT U.S. OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS ROARS BACK INTO HUNT AT U.S. OPEN.

text.p: The sounds of a Tiger on the prowl rumbled through Congressional Country Club early Friday morning as Masters champion Woods got back into the U.S. Open hunt with four birdies on the front nine.

Woods, whose four-over-par 74 on Thursday had left him a massive nine strokes behind leader Colin Montgomerie, wasted little time in getting rid of the bad taste of his floundering first-round finish.
The 21-year-old Woods was on target with his irons on a steamy, overcast day that held the threat of rain.
Woods birdied the first, third, fifth and seventh holes -- all from within five feet -- to reach level par for the tournament.
With Montgomerie two hours away from teeing off for the second round, the only player to threaten his standing in the very early going was British Open champion Tom Lehman.

Lehman, who began the day at three under par, struggled at first with bogeys at numbers two and three. But, perhaps inspired by the birdie binge by playing partner Woods, he birdied five, eight and nine to reach four-under.
A bogey at the 10th pulled Lehman back to where he started, at three under par.
Another contender making a charge was 1994 champion Ernie Els. The strapping South African made four birdies on the frontside to reach three under par.
Birdies were not available to everyone, of course, on a layout that produced only nine rounds under par from the 156- player field on Thursday.
Steve Stricker, joint second after his first-round 66, double-bogeyed the fourth hole to drop to two under par.

John Daly, playing his first major championship since undergoing his latest treatment for alcoholism, withdrew from the Open after nine holes on Friday. He had carded three bogeys on the day and stood at 10 over par for the tournament.
Dave Schreyer, fresh from the satellite Hooters Tour, did not have much chance to enjoy the two-under-par 68 that had left him joint sixth after the first round.
The Georgian started his round on Friday with bogey-bogey- double bogey to topple from the leaderboard.
Taking Schreyer's place as an outsider with a hot hand was Scott Dunlap, who matched Woods's brilliant front side of four-under 31.
Dunlap, who has missed eight cuts on the U.S. tour this year, had two more birdies after the turn to haul himself up to one under par after starting the day at five-over.
The true test for Woods was coming on the back nine, where the young star had struggled to a pair of double bogeys and two bogeys in his first round.
Steve Stricker, like Sutton, had also shot a four-under 66 in the opening round but could not keep pace Friday.
The 30-year-old Stricker, whose wife Nicki caddies for him, double-bogeyed the fourth when his lipped-out, par-putt from six feet spun four feet away.
He missed the putt coming back and took a double bogey, the first of three doubles that sent him plummeting off the leaderboard.
At three under par along with Lehman was Mark McNulty of Zimbabwe, who also had not yet teed off for his second round.

The delay in play was sure to keep a number of groups from being able to finish their rounds Friday and it was expected they would be asked to return to Congressional early Saturday morning to complete them.
Only nine players managed to break par on Thursday over the 7,213-yard, par-70 layout that is the longest ever to hold a U.S. Open.
Scoring was easier Friday as some light early morning rain and a brief heavy shower during the suspension helped soften the course.

The low round Friday among the early starters was turned in by journeyman pro Scott Dunlap, who registered a four-under 66. Dunlap, who began the day at five over par, had gotten to six-under for the round before two late bogeys.
"It's very soft out there, the greens and the fairways," said Lehman. "The course is still in great shape and the greens are holding up. I expect to see some low scores."
Despite his wobbly finish, Woods was pleased with his round.
"The key is to keep getting better every day and you'll be there at the end," he said. "I'm back in the tournament.
"The only thing I'm concerned about is to get myself under par and into contention on Sunday."
Els said he was bothered somewhat by the slow pace of play, which was aggravated by the sudden departure of playing partner John Daly, who walked off the course after nine holes.
"I like to play fast. I like to walk up to my ball, get the yardage and then hit it. But we couldn't do that most of the back nine," said Els.
Els was left to play in a twosome with Payne Stewart after Daly departed.

Daly, who has returned to competitive golf after a recent eight-week rehabilitation programme for treatment of alcoholism, later issued a statement saying he had withdrawn from the tournament because of mental and physical fatigue.
